items.prompt_md: After one partition step around a pivot value, what do you know about the pivot's position?
options: It is somewhere random; only the pivot's side is sorted
It is at its final sorted position, with no larger values to its left and no smaller values to its right
It is always at the end of the array
items.answer: It is at its final sorted position, with no larger values to its left and no smaller values to its right
items.explanation_md: That guarantee is what lets quickselect compare the target index to the pivot's index and discard one side. The pivot is not necessarily the median, and the sides themselves are still unsorted.

items.prompt_md: For an array of length `n`, which ascending-order index holds the k-th **largest** element?
items.answer: `n - k`
items.explanation_md: The largest is at index `n - 1` (k = 1 gives `n - 1`), the second largest at `n - 2`, and so on. `k - 1` is the index of the k-th **smallest**.

items.prompt_md: After partitioning, the target index is smaller than the start of the pivot block. What does quickselect do next?
options: Recurse into the left side only
Recurse into the right side only
items.answer: Recurse into the left side only
items.explanation_md: Everything left of the pivot block is smaller, and the target index lies there. Visiting only one side is exactly why quickselect is O(n) on average instead of O(n log n).

items.prompt_md: Why is the pivot chosen at random?
options: It is required for the partition to be correct
It makes the O(n^2) worst case highly unlikely for any fixed input, including sorted or adversarial ones
It lets the algorithm use less than O(1) extra space
items.answer: It makes the O(n^2) worst case highly unlikely for any fixed input, including sorted or adversarial ones
items.explanation_md: Any pivot value gives a correct partition, so correctness never depends on randomness. A fixed rule (like always the first element) is quadratic on already sorted input; a random choice avoids that.

items.prompt_md: What are the average and worst-case time of quickselect?
options: O(n log n) average, O(n log n) worst
items.answer: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst
items.explanation_md: On average the range halves each round, so the scans total about n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n. If every pivot is the extreme value, each round removes one element and the total is n + (n-1) + ... = O(n^2).

items.prompt_md: What is the time and extra space of the size-k min-heap solution for the k-th largest of an array of `n` elements?
options: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
O(k log n) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(1) space
items.answer: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
items.explanation_md: Each of the `n` elements triggers at most one push and one pop on a heap capped at `k`, so O(log k) each. The heap holds `k` items. The O(n) / O(1) option is quickselect.

items.prompt_md: The iterative quickselect rearranges the array in place using a few index variables. What is its extra space, and what does a **recursive** version add?
options: O(n) extra space; recursion adds nothing
O(1) extra space; recursion adds stack depth, expected O(log n) and worst O(n)
O(k) extra space; recursion adds O(k)
items.answer: O(1) extra space; recursion adds stack depth, expected O(log n) and worst O(n)
items.explanation_md: The loop keeps only `lo`, `hi` and a few pointers. A recursive version holds one frame per round, so its depth follows the number of rounds. The call stack counts as space.

items.prompt_md: Which sort is O(n log n) in the worst case, stable, and uses O(n) extra space?
items.answer: Merge sort
items.explanation_md: Merge sort halves recursively and merges in linear time with a temporary buffer; merging keeps equal keys in order. Quicksort is O(n^2) worst and unstable, heap sort is in place but unstable, selection sort is O(n^2).

items.prompt_md: A two-way (Lomuto) partition splits into `< pivot` and `>= pivot`. On an array where every element is equal, what happens to quickselect using it?
options: Each round removes only one element, so the time degrades to O(n^2)
items.answer: Each round removes only one element, so the time degrades to O(n^2)
items.explanation_md: Everything lands on the `>=` side, leaving a range one smaller each round. The answer is still correct. A 3-way partition groups all copies of the pivot into a middle block and finishes in one pass.

items.prompt_md: In the Dutch-flag 3-way partition, after swapping `nums[i]` with `nums[gt]` because `nums[i] > pivot`, why is `i` **not** incremented?
options: To keep the loop running forever
The value swapped in from `gt` has not been examined yet and could be smaller or equal
items.answer: The value swapped in from `gt` has not been examined yet and could be smaller or equal
items.explanation_md: The region at and beyond `gt + 1` is already known to be greater, but the element arriving at `i` came from the unexamined zone. When swapping with `lt` instead, the value arriving at `i` is a known-equal element, so `i` can advance.

items.prompt_md: What does quickselect do to the caller's input array?
options: Nothing; it works on a copy by definition
Reorders it in place, so copy first if the original order matters
items.answer: Reorders it in place, so copy first if the original order matters
items.explanation_md: Partitioning swaps elements in the original list. It is not fully sorted afterwards, only partially arranged around the pivots tried. Mentioning the mutation is a good interview habit.

items.prompt_md: Given a fixed array of up to a million integers, report the 5000th smallest, using as little extra memory as possible. The array may be modified. Which technique fits?
options: A size-5000 max-heap kept while scanning
Quickselect with a random pivot, iteratively
items.answer: Quickselect with a random pivot, iteratively
items.explanation_md: A static array, a single rank, and a memory limit with permission to mutate point to in-place selection at O(n) average and O(1) extra. The heap would need O(5000) memory and O(n log k) time.

items.prompt_md: Orders stream in forever and you must always know the 10th highest order value, without storing everything. Which technique fits?
options: A size-10 min-heap updated per order
items.answer: A size-10 min-heap updated per order
items.explanation_md: Streams cannot be re-partitioned cheaply each time, and storing all orders is not allowed. A bounded heap answers in O(log 10) per order with fixed memory.

items.prompt_md: You are asked to implement a general-purpose sort for integers and told stability does not matter but extra memory should be minimal. Which choice is the best answer?
options: Quicksort with a random pivot, in place, expected O(n log n)
Merge sort with a full-size auxiliary buffer
Counting sort over the full integer range
items.answer: Quicksort with a random pivot, in place, expected O(n log n)
items.explanation_md: Stability not needed and memory tight favours in-place quicksort (or heap sort for a worst-case guarantee). Merge sort uses O(n) space; counting sort is only sensible for a small value range.

items.prompt_md: A set of 2D points is given, and you need the 3 closest to the origin. The input may be reordered and no stream is involved. Which technique fits?
options: Quickselect on squared distance, then take the first 3
items.answer: Quickselect on squared distance, then take the first 3
items.explanation_md: Quickselect puts the k smallest keys before index `k` in O(n) average, with no sort of the rest. A size-k max-heap is the alternative when streaming. Squared distance avoids square roots.

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted array and a rank `k`, return the k-th smallest element. Which approach is best?
items.answer: Index directly into position `k - 1`
items.explanation_md: The order is already known, so the answer is a constant-time lookup. Selection algorithms matter only for unsorted input.

items.prompt_md: You need the median of a live data stream after each new value. Which technique fits?
options: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
items.answer: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
items.explanation_md: Rerunning quickselect would cost O(n) per query. Two heaps give O(log n) insert and O(1) median, and the data keeps changing, so a one-off sort is wrong.

items.prompt_md: Given sorted lists from several servers, return the 100 smallest values overall. Which technique fits?
options: A min-heap holding the front of each list, popped 100 times
items.answer: A min-heap holding the front of each list, popped 100 times
items.explanation_md: The sources are already sorted, so a merge frontier extracts the smallest values lazily in O(100 log lists). Concatenating and selecting discards the existing order and touches every item.

items.prompt_md: A function `ok(x)` is monotone in `x` (false then true), and you need the smallest integer in `[0, 10^9]` where it is true. Which technique fits?
items.answer: Binary search on the answer
items.explanation_md: A monotone predicate over an ordered range is the textbook binary-search signal; there is no collection to partition. Selection algorithms rank existing items, not search a predicate's boundary.

items.prompt_md: You need to know whether an array contains any duplicate value. Which technique fits?
options: A heap of the smallest k values
A hash set seen so far
Merge two halves recursively with a heap
items.answer: A hash set seen so far
items.explanation_md: Duplicate detection is membership, answered in O(n) with a set. Ranking or ordering tools like selection and sorting are unnecessary (sorting would work but costs O(n log n)).

items.prompt_md: Find the largest sum of any contiguous block of exactly 4 consecutive values in an array. Which technique fits?
options: Sort the array and add the last 4
A fixed-size sliding window with a running sum
A min-heap of sums of all subsets
items.answer: A fixed-size sliding window with a running sum
items.explanation_md: The block must be contiguous, so sorting destroys the structure and quickselect ranks the wrong thing. A window updated in O(1) per step is the fit.
